stories.headline: Revolut puts ~2,000 engineers on self-hosted GLM-5.3 across 56 Nvidia B200s, cutting AI coding costs ~90%
stories.why_read: A regulated fintech shows what unlimited cheap tokens look like in production: less Claude spend, more Jira debugging, and a router that still peels vision work to closed models.
body: At AI Engineer NYC, Revolut AI ops lead David Abitbol said the company made self-hosted open-weight GLM models the default coding stack for roughly 2,000 engineers. Revolut started on GLM-5.1 in April 2026 and later moved to GLM-5.3, serving it from 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. The Register's write-up of the talk puts blended cost near $0.30 per million tokens — about a tenth of prior Anthropic and OpenAI spend — and cites a ~60% improvement in coding time and ~70% in lead time after the AI rollout (with the usual caveat that the charts do not isolate the model change alone).

The interesting part is the serving recipe, not the GPU count. Abitbol described NVFP4 quantization, disaggregated prefill/decode, and a practical 256K context sweet spot (he called million-token windows a scam for their workload), landing sub-3-second time-to-first-token and ~200 tokens/s interactive generation. GLM stays text-only, so a router still sends vision work to Gemini or GPT Luna, and Claude/Codex remain for exceptions. For anyone running coding agents at company scale, this is the clearest public data point yet on self-hosted economics.

stories.headline: Anthropic's amended S-1 puts ~$895B of compute and data-center commitments on the table
stories.why_read: The IPO filing turns AI's power bill into hard numbers — and puts Broadcom, Google, SpaceX's AI unit and Amazon at the front of the queue.
body: Anthropic's amended IPO filing lists about $895 billion of purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all for compute and infrastructure, according to Yahoo Finance's read of the S-1 update and matching SEC language. Roughly $70 billion comes due within a year, and nearly $450 billion by the end of 2030. The cash and short-term investments on hand at the end of September were about $132 billion, so the commitment stack is nearly seven times the liquid balance sheet.

On the supplier side, Broadcom leads with about $161 billion in equipment leases, Google about $121 billion, SpaceX's AI unit up to $120.5 billion, and Amazon $110 billion. Separate plans for another $125–150 billion of Google chips and more than $20 billion with AMD are not counted in the $895 billion because they lack fixed dollar commitments. Third-quarter revenue jumped to about $17 billion, but Anthropic swung back to a $567 million operating loss after one profitable quarter — a reminder that the rent still runs ahead of the rent check.

stories.headline: Claude Code was putting users' email addresses into User-Agent headers on web requests
stories.why_read: A 1,200-point HN thread that turns agent reliability into a privacy incident — and a live case study in why harness invariants beat vibe-coded guardrails.
body: GitHub issue #107757 reports that Claude Code 2.1.318 on macOS sent the signed-in account email in User-Agent headers while doing web searches and curl-style calls. An Anthropic engineer said the email was added to model context so Claude would stop hallucinating @author tags, then sometimes reused it as a contact address when sites ask agents to identify themselves. A built-in cc-plugin-privacy mod shipped in 2.1.317+ to block some of those cases, and a follow-up on HN says the account email will be removed from model context in a release early next week.

Users on 2.1.318 still reported gaps — scripts written by the agent, echo tests that should have been denied, and spam inboxes that suddenly woke up. The thread is as much about harness design as the leak itself: reliability arguments meet subagent failure modes when the agent invents its own network identity. If you run Claude Code in a fleet, patch promptly and treat email-in-context as hostile until the next release lands.

stories.headline: METR: Anthropic's model capabilities are improving ~1.9× faster than before, likely mostly from AI-assisted R&D
stories.why_read: The first high-access outside look at whether AI is actually speeding up AI research — with redactions, caveats, and a 1.9× AECI slope change since October 2025.
body: METR spent August 12 to October 29 inside Anthropic assessing AI R&D acceleration and published its public conclusions on November 5. On Anthropic's AECI capability index, benchmark scores have grown at an estimated 1.9× the pre-October 2025 rate (95% CI 1.5–2.8×), implying roughly two years of historical progress in the last year. Most METR staff on the project now believe Anthropic is improving capabilities on well-specified tasks at around twice the March 2024–October 2025 rate, with a wide personal uncertainty band from about 1.3× to 3×.

METR is confident the speedup is not from faster training-compute scaling, and guesses a majority of today's acceleration is from extensive AI use in R&D — while noting Anthropic redacted a majority of the most informative evidence. Staff Slack polls of self-reported uplift reached about 12× for the most capable internal model in October 2026, though METR treats those as loose evidence. No clear bottlenecks on algorithms, compute, or data showed up for the next 12 months, which is exactly the compounding-risk scenario safety teams worry about.

stories.headline: Hyperstition open-sources Hyperkernel megakernels it says beat NVIDIA's published DeepSeek V4.1 Flash vLLM numbers
stories.why_read: An MIT-licensed alpha that fuses whole model forwards into one GPU launch — vendor benchmarks, B300-only for now, generator still forthcoming.
body: Hyperstition published generated megakernels under MIT at github.com/Hyperstitioncc/Hyperkernel. The alpha Hyperserve binary targets NVIDIA B300s (four GPUs for LLMs), needs Rust and driver R580+, and serves DeepSeek V4.1 Flash behind an OpenAI-compatible API. The company's own thread claims 36.7% higher per-user generation speed at concurrency 1 and 90.6% at concurrency 4 versus NVIDIA's published vLLM results on the same model, plus robotics and genomics kernels (π₀-FAST, ACT, Evo 2, ESMFold) produced in under an hour for some domains.

Treat the speedups as vendor claims until independent runs land. The full Hyperkernel generator and promised Kimi/GLM serving stacks are still weeks out, and the released builds are B300-specific even though the company says generation extends to B200, AMD and TPUs. For inference teams, the useful signal is the megakernel bet itself: one persistent launch instead of a graph of ops, aimed at batch-one latency where launch overhead dominates.

stories.headline: Thinking Machines ships Inkling 2 Small: a 594B MoE (17B active) headed for Apache 2.0 weights
stories.why_read: A multimodal coding-and-vision model that posts an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index of 31 and promises open weights after a week of safety testing.
body: Thinking Machines Lab introduced Inkling 2 Small on November 5: a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion total parameters, 17 billion active, image inputs, variable effort, and up to a 1M-token context. It scores 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and is initially available closed-weights on Tinker for inference and fine-tuning, with full Apache 2.0 weights planned after external safety testing and red-teaming next week.

The post leans hard on agentic coding and autoresearch — RL over hundreds of thousands of long-horizon tasks, a from-scratch city simulator and a Python PC emulator in the demos, and a time-series forecasting run that more than doubled a Qwen3.5-4B baseline after 4.5 hours and $426 of Tinker spend. Pretraining used NVFP4 on GB300 NVL72 racks; the main RL run burned over 4×10²³ FLOPs across 2,048 GPUs and 17M+ rollouts. Until the weights drop, treat the open-weight crown as pending.

stories.headline: Agility Robotics begins Nasdaq trading as AGLT, the first U.S. pure-play listed humanoid company with live deployments
stories.why_read: Digit already works in warehouses; the public listing puts a price on commercial humanoids just as Tesla Optimus and the rest of the field race for scale.
body: Agility Robotics started trading on Nasdaq on November 5 under AGLT (warrants AGLTW) after completing its SPAC combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The company calls itself the first U.S. publicly listed pure-play humanoid robotics firm with proven commercial deployments. The deal and related financings raised about $465 million in gross capital before expenses.

Digit has logged more than 65,000 hours at customers including GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Agility cites more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5 (subject to contractual milestones and specs), with early access targeted for the first half of 2027. Digit 5 is designed to lift up to 50 pounds, swap end effectors, and recharge in about nine minutes for more than 20 hours of work in a day. For autonomy watchers who already track Cybercab drills in Texas, this is the public-markets twin.

stories.headline: Anthropic's biology lab uses Claude to map the first 3D prokaryotic vault particle
stories.why_read: A concrete Claude-in-the-loop structural biology win: 96-copy phage vault, 34-hour first model, and a purification that collapsed from days to ~90 minutes.
body: Anthropic's science team reports the first 3D structure of a vault particle from a prokaryotic system — specifically a bacteriophage protein they call L05. Cryo-EM shows a ~9.5-megadalton shell of 96 protein copies (48 per half), about 54 by 45 nanometers, shorter and wider than mammalian vaults and enclosing roughly 25% more volume. Vaults have been known in eukaryotes since 1986 with no settled function; related genes had been spotted in bacteria and phages, but assembly into actual vaults had not been shown.

Claude helped search ~15 billion predicted proteins, design DNA constructs, optimize size-exclusion isolation, and drive RELION processing. Isolation that normally takes about three days landed in ~90 minutes; a first full model was ready in 34 hours. The team also engineered a longer vault by duplicating wall repeats (~20% more volume) and found an unidentified pocket ligand that resembles coenzyme A. Function is still open — Leonard Rome, who discovered vaults, is advising — but the methods post is a clear template for agentic wet-lab acceleration.

stories.headline: Cursor can now build and publish live web apps from a cloud agent — database, auth and hosting included
stories.why_read: The localhost-to-link gap just closed for anyone already living in Cursor Cloud Agents, which matches the deploy muscle Anand has been RTing.
body: Cursor's November 5 changelog says you can tell a cloud agent to build an app and it will scaffold the web app, provision Postgres if needed, put auth behind Cursor SSO, and host it. Publish picks a unique domain, runs deterministic and agentic security checks (secrets in files, credential files, .env, source maps), and only goes live after you explicitly confirm. Paid plans with cloud agents get it; team admins can audit every app and secret.

Apps can start from a new Cursor Origin repo or an existing GitHub repo. Sharing is invite-only, team-wide, or public on individual plans, and API keys let scripts or Grok Bot hit private apps without a browser login. It is the natural complement to one-click deploy muscle in Anand's timeline: describe the tool, get a shareable URL, keep the secrets out of the prompt.

stories.headline: Bryan Cantrill's Rust NYC talk: 'Code Matters: Reflections on Rust in the LLM Age'
stories.why_read: A systems elder makes the case that Rust's compile-time honesty matters more, not less, when agents are writing the diffs.
body: Bryan Cantrill's Rust NYC talk 'Code Matters: Reflections on Rust in the LLM Age' is circulating again in engineer timelines (Anand among them). The Speaker Deck deck argues that Rust's strict, compile-time-checked design is especially valuable when LLMs generate code, while warning that models often prefer complex solutions over simple abstractions a human can still hold in their head.

It pairs cleanly with the reliability chatter on the same timeline — arguments that agent-written code should be more reliable, and that subagents are a top failure mode. If your shop is letting Claude Code or Codex own larger PRs, Cantrill's framing is a useful brake: prefer languages and APIs that make the machine prove its work before merge.

stories.headline: Science's Last Exam launches with 113 research tasks; FrontierPhysics shows top agents still below 30% pass
stories.why_read: Two serious attempts to grade whether agents can do real science — not quiz questions — land in the same news cycle.
body: Science's Last Exam (SLE), led by the AItonomy Foundation with researchers from 34 institutions, launches November 6 with 113 public tasks across nine disciplines. Agents get a research goal and tools, not a worked example, and are graded on sealed deterministic checks plus capability diagnostics (hypothesis discovery, protocol planning, scientific computing, and more). Wet-lab execution is still in construction.

Alongside it, FrontierPhysics posts 56 end-to-end physics tasks built by 42 physicists from their own research. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no setup passed more than 46 of 168 rollouts; Claude Opus 5.5 led at 27.4% Pass@1. Manual review of GPT-6 Astra trajectories blamed weak rigorous reasoning and missing expert intuition more than missing textbook knowledge. If you have been waiting for benchmarks that feel like PI assignments instead of multiple choice, these are the ones.

stories.headline: Notion open-sources Lore, a shared persistent memory vault for AI agents
stories.why_read: Tribal knowledge that used to die in a single agent session can now live in Notion databases both humans and MCP agents can read.
body: Notion's engineering blog describes Lore, an MIT-licensed shared memory system backed by Notion pages and databases (Projects, Topics, Memories, Entities, Facts). Agents reach it through lore-* MCP tools; humans use the same pages in Notion or a CLI. The pitch is multiplayer: agents on one desk learn from agents on another, capturing experiential knowledge, follow-ups, decision records and rare procedures that skills files never quite absorb.

Facts expire unless reinforced, and relations like supersedes / conflicts_with keep the vault from becoming a junk drawer. On SkillRet retrieval, Lore hit 84% success on 500 sampled queries; on hard paired coding tasks, seeded memory lifted pass rates with a McNemar p of 0.0008 and recovered about 46% of no-memory failures. An internal pilot still found plenty of duplicates and inferable fluff — memory quality remains the product.

stories.headline: AI-linked stocks sold off hard on November 5 as midterm and spending worries hit the Nasdaq
stories.why_read: A single session that priced in both political risk to data centers and fatigue with AI capex — useful context beside Anthropic's $895B commitment stack.
body: U.S. tech shares tumbled on November 5 as investors fretted that Democratic midterm gains could slow data-center buildouts and tighten AI regulation, while also reassessing the return on massive AI infrastructure spend. Contemporary wire coverage put the Nasdaq down about 5.5% into correction territory and the S&P 500 down about 4.4%, with chips, memory and AI-infrastructure names leading the drop.

The tape sits next to this week's Anthropic S-1 compute commitments and the still-fresh local ballot fights over data centers. Bubble-fear headlines travel faster than balance-sheet nuance, but for anyone allocating GPUs or power, the signal is that equity markets are no longer giving AI buildout a free pass.

stories.headline: Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) shows up on HN as another bid to make GPU clusters feel like normal K8s
stories.why_read: If you already herd B200s for coding agents, a thinner path from YAML to scheduled GPUs is worth a look.
body: An open project branded Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) hit the Hacker News front page from github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke. The repo positions itself as tooling to run and schedule NVIDIA GPU workloads on Kubernetes with less bespoke glue — the perennial pain point once you move past a single DGX and into multi-node inference or RL farms.

Details and maturity vary by commit, so read the README before you bet a cluster on it. Still, between Revolut's 56-B200 coding fleet and Anthropic's commitment stack, the ops layer around GPUs is suddenly as newsy as the models themselves.

stories.headline: MS Paint picks up a remote code execution CVE: CVE-2026-83844
stories.why_read: A reminder that even the oldest Windows inbox apps still sit on the exploit path.
body: CVE-2026-83844, listed on cve.org and climbing Hacker News, covers a remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft Paint. Paint has been a punchline for decades; an RCE against it is a reminder that inbox Windows binaries remain high-value targets precisely because users still open random images without thinking.

Patch calendars and enterprise image pipelines should treat this like any other Office-adjacent client bug: confirm the KB, stage it, and do not assume 'we disabled Paint' is a real control. Full technical detail belongs on the CVE record and Microsoft's advisory once mirrored.

stories.headline: Blender's UI and runtime are being held up as much faster than GPUI
stories.why_read: A sharp HN thread for anyone building native UI stacks and wondering whether the new Rust UI kits are actually winning on speed.
body: A GitHub project comparing Blender's UI/runtime path to GPUI landed near the top of Hacker News with the blunt claim that Blender's approach is much faster. The post is less a product launch than a performance provocation aimed at the wave of GPU-accelerated UI frameworks.

If you are choosing a desktop shell for an agent IDE or internal tool, the useful takeaway is to benchmark realistic editor workloads — text, panels, continuous redraw — rather than trusting framework marketing. Blender's decades of viewport work are a high bar.

stories.headline: Dutch bank ASN blocks non-Google Android devices, including GrapheneOS
stories.why_read: A concrete clash between hardened Android and banking apps that demand Google's attestation stack.
body: A PrivSec banking-apps compatibility report issue documents Dutch 'idealist' bank ASN blocking non-Google Android builds, GrapheneOS included. The pattern is familiar: apps that lean on Google Play Integrity / SafetyNet-style signals quietly lock out de-Googled phones even when the device is more locked down than stock.

For privacy-minded Android users it is another data point that the hard part of leaving Google is not the ROM — it is the banks, rideshare apps and government portals that outsource trust to Play Services. Track the issue thread for workarounds and which other EU banks follow.

stories.headline: Ashlee Vance profiles 21-year-old Naman Pushp, building carbon-fiber cargo aircraft at Airbound in Bengaluru
stories.why_read: A Core Memory visit to India's hard-tech bench: YouTube-taught composites, VTOL cargo birds, and a bet that aviation underuses carbon fiber.
body: Ashlee Vance's Core Memory episode and write-up introduce Naman Pushp, 21-year-old founder of Airbound in Bengaluru. Pushp taught himself carbon-fiber aircraft construction from YouTube, skipped Carnegie Mellon to keep building, and now flies VTOL cargo aircraft designed around composites rather than treating carbon fiber as a metal substitute.

Vance watched dozens of the quiet, hovering machines at Airbound's test sites and frames Pushp as part of a generation of Indian founders choosing domestic hard tech over copycat SaaS. The company still has a long way to go from package delivery to anything passenger-shaped, but the materials thesis is the hook.

stories.headline: sshole: the mischievous SSH honeypot that made HN's front page
stories.why_read: A 2,700-point distraction that still teaches something about who is knocking on port 22.
body: sshole.com rocketed up Hacker News with a playful take on SSH honeypots — bait for the endless credential-stuffing noise that hits any public port 22. High score aside, it is a useful reminder to keep real SSH behind keys, fail2ban or a VPN, and to treat internet-wide scans as background radiation.
Use it as comic relief between CVE write-ups, not as your production detection stack.

stories.headline: The Hackintosh reborn — with AI along for the ride
stories.why_read: A nostalgic hardware essay for anyone who ever fought kexts, now rewritten for the agent era.
body: A naut.ca post titled 'The Hackintosh Reborn' walks through building a modern Hackintosh with AI assistance in the loop. It is part memoir, part how-to, and it landed solidly on HN for readers who miss OpenCore late nights.

Apple Silicon closed the classic Hackintosh chapter for many; this piece is about why people still bother on Intel boards and how coding agents change the debugging grind. Read for the vibe as much as the parts list.

stories.headline: Show HN: Firenook — Firebase emulators in Rust claiming 40× faster writes and 10× less RAM
stories.why_read: If your integration tests still wait on the official Firebase emulator, a Rust rewrite promising order-of-magnitude speedups is worth a weekend spike.
body: Firenook.dev hit Show HN pitching Firebase emulators rewritten in Rust, with claimed 40× faster writes and 10× less RAM than the stock emulator stack. Local emulator pain is a perennial tax on mobile and serverless teams; a drop-in that is actually fast would change CI shape.
As with any Show HN systems claim, verify against your own workload before rewriting pipelines. The project page and HN thread are the place to start.

stories.headline: September in Servo: progress bars, rounded rectangles, and more engine polish
stories.why_read: A quiet monthly reminder that an independent Rust browser engine is still shipping tangible UI primitives.
body: Servo's September 2026 update covers new support for HTML progress elements, rounded rectangles, and assorted rendering and layout polish. The project remains the most serious open Rust browser engine effort outside the Chromium/WebKit duopoly.

None of it is a headline browser launch, but the cadence matters: embedding and research users need boring monthly progress more than splashy demos. Read the post if you track alternative engine health.

stories.headline: Motorola Signature 27 ships with GrapheneOS support
stories.why_read: A mainstream OEM nodding at the hardened Android niche — rare enough to note beside ASN's GrapheneOS block.
body: Motorola News reports the Signature 27 with GrapheneOS support, a contrast to the same day's HN thread about ASN Bank locking GrapheneOS users out. OEM-blessed unlockable devices remain the scarce ingredient for private Android.

Availability, bootloader policy and which radios stay locked will decide whether this is real progress or marketing. Still, pairing an OEM announcement with a bank block makes the privacy-phone story of the day.

stories.headline: Goldman and Apollo start selling slices of SpaceX's record $40 billion GPU financing
stories.why_read: A look at how AI compute is now financed: off-balance-sheet chip leases priced like corporate debt.
body: Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management are marketing portions of up to $500 million from SpaceX's record $40 billion GPU financing to investors ahead of full syndication, according to X's summary. In the structure, an Apollo special-purpose vehicle buys Nvidia Rubin chips and equipment, funded by debt and a $7 billion lease prepayment from SpaceX. SpaceX then rents the hardware for five years, keeping the obligation off its balance sheet.

The tranches include an $8.3 billion senior loan priced at 215 basis points over Treasuries and bonds at up to 395 basis points, with hardware deliveries starting in early 2027 to feed SpaceX's AI compute alongside Starlink and launches. Observers note strong investor demand despite jitters in the AI debt market. The roundup also notes SpaceX shares dipped 3.8% amid election reactions.

stories.headline: OpenAI's cyber pipeline found 948 working Linux kernel root exploits for about $1,279 each
stories.why_read: An AI pipeline producing kernel privilege escalations at industrial scale changes the threat model for every shared Linux host you run.
body: In 'A thousand fewer paths to root,' OpenAI describes an autonomous pipeline built on an upcoming cyber model and pointed at the Linux kernel. Scouts identified 5,034 targets covering about 2.8 million lines of code, roughly 7% of the kernel. From 2,308 candidate bugs the system reproduced 1,724 and produced 948 unique local privilege escalation exploits plus 291 info-leak proofs of concept, at a total cost of $1,213,430, or about $1,279 per LPE. OpenAI says the run surfaced at least ten novel exploitation techniques. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Sol found 166 LPEs for $513,690 in July.

The fixes are moving through the kernel: within ten days, 61 had been patched upstream and 43 more were in staging, as part of OpenAI's Patch the Planet and Daybreak efforts. The post's blunt operational advice is to treat a low-privileged account on an unpatched OS as root-equivalent, and to isolate untrusted workloads with microVMs or sandboxes such as Firecracker or gVisor rather than relying on container boundaries alone.

stories.headline: Anthropic shows zkSNARK proofs that a response really came from the model you were promised
stories.why_read: If you've ever wondered whether a router quietly swapped in a cheaper model, this is the cryptographic answer, built largely by Claude.
body: Anthropic researchers, working with collaborators from EPFL, StarkWare, MIT and Succinct, describe FlashProve, a zkSNARK system for provable inference. A provider commits to a model and then proves that each response was produced by that model, without revealing the weights. On Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B-parameter mixture of experts with 4-bit weights, a single H100 generates proofs at around 110 tokens per second, with a proof of about 19 MB per 1,024-token request. That is roughly 70 to 95 times the GPU time of serving the model on vLLM, which the team says is orders of magnitude faster than prior open-source systems.

The twist is that Claude did much of the optimization work. Because its design choices can be hard to audit, the team pinned the top-level security claims in Lean formal statements. They released the blog post, a technical report, a Claude-written protocol specification, and code that includes a prover, a fast C++ verifier and a provably correct verifier. The pitch spans consumer trust, internal security and compliance checks on AI pacing rules.

stories.headline: AMD guides to about $17 billion in Q4 revenue, enough to outsell Intel for the first time ever
stories.why_read: A historic crossover driven almost entirely by data center CPUs and AI accelerators, which is exactly the hardware you buy.
body: AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.377 billion, up from $9.25 billion a year earlier and $11.54 billion the previous quarter, with a 54% gross margin and net income up 95% to $2.43 billion, according to Tom's Hardware. The Data Center segment reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% year over year, with operating margin expanding from 25% to 34%. Data center now makes up 64% of AMD's revenue, on the strength of Epyc processors and Instinct accelerators.

The headline is the outlook. AMD expects fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, while Intel guided to $15 billion to $16 billion amid weak PC demand and manufacturing constraints. If both companies land near their midpoints, AMD's quarterly sales would top Intel's by about $1.5 billion for the first time in history. The caveat in the report is that AMD's client and gaming businesses face double-digit declines going into 2027, as high memory prices weigh on PCs.

stories.headline: Drone views over Giga Texas show Cybercabs running traffic drills as a chip fab and Optimus factory rise
stories.why_read: Your Austin neighbor in aerial form: Cybercab testing, new fab steel and a move to round-the-clock shifts, all visible from the sky.
body: Fresh drone footage over Giga Texas, highlighted by longtime site watchers Joe Tegtmeyer and Herbert Ong, shows groups of Cybercabs practicing traffic scenarios on the test track, stopping at lights and reacting to one another in coordinated runs alongside Model Y test vehicles. The same flyovers capture steel going up for a chip fab, growth at the Optimus factory and a new cooling plant on the campus.

X's summary also reports that the factory is shifting to 24-hour operations with two 12-hour shifts to push output through year-end, with minimal holiday downtime. None of this is an official Tesla announcement, so treat timelines with care. Still, it's a rare chance to watch robotaxi, robotics and silicon work happening in parallel on one site a short drive from home.

stories.headline: Voters reject data centers in 46 of 47 local ballot measures
stories.why_read: The midterms delivered a clear verdict on the physical side of the AI boom, and Texas is next in line for the same fight.
body: X's news summary of Tuesday's results says voters approved limits or outright bans on data centers in 46 of 47 local ballot measures, in states including Ohio, California and Florida. The concerns cited were power and water demand, rising electricity bills and quality-of-life impacts on nearby neighborhoods. Tech advocates pushed back by pointing to medical uses of AI such as mapping tumors and finding drug synergies, while surveys cited in the roundup show broad, cross-party support for more government oversight of AI and data centers.

Texas has its own version of the debate. Senator-elect James Talarico said in a clip posted Wednesday that data center companies must pay for their own energy so they don't drive up utility bills, recycle their own water and get the consent of the communities they build in. The investor @Jason replied that this is 'completely reasonable and exactly what the data center industry is doing,' and urged towns that land a data center to extract as much as they can for local schools and playgrounds. For anyone planning capacity, the takeaway is that power and community consent are now as much of a gating factor as GPUs.

stories.headline: Moonshot releases Kimi K3.1 Pro weights: a 2.8-trillion-parameter agentic MoE that trades blows with Claude Opus 5.5
stories.why_read: The strongest open-weight agentic model to land this fall, and its coding scores sit within a point of the closed frontier.
body: Moonshot AI has published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face as an open-weight, natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model built for agentic work. The model card lists 2.8 trillion total parameters with 104 billion active per token, 896 experts with 16 selected per token, a 1M-token context window and weights shipped in MXFP4. Architecturally, the card says Gated DSA attention replaces Gated MLA.

The benchmark table is the reason it hit 555 points on Hacker News. Kimi K3.1 Pro posts 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 66.4 for Claude Opus 5.5, scores 51.7 on SWE Marathon (the best number in Moonshot's comparison), 92.1 on BrowseComp and 70.0 on Humanity's Last Exam with tools. It ships under a custom Kimi K3.1 Pro License rather than a standard open-source license, so read the terms before planning a deployment, and at this size self-hosting is a serious cluster job, not a weekend project.
